newsitem.title: FRANCE: Balladur urges French to avoid power-sharing.
newsitem.headline: Balladur urges French to avoid power-sharing.

text.p: Former French prime minister Edouard Balladur urged voters on Thursday not to force France back down the road of power-sharing by electing a left-wing government under conservative President Jacques Chirac.
Balladur, who led a conservative government under late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand for two years, warned of conflict between European and domestic issues.
But he disagreed with some who saw power-sharing between a president and government of rival parties -- or "cohabitation" as it is known in France -- as a threat to the political system.

Speaking in a radio interview, he also refused to be drawn on his own chances of being prime minister if the centre-right coalition recovers from a first-round setback to win Sunday's decisive vote in early parliamentary elections.

"I do not want there to be a cohabitation...because if it becomes inevitable, it reduces the efficiency of government actions -- less so on domestic policy than external policy," Balladur told France Inter radio.

France's Fifth Republic constitution gives the president responsibility for foreign policy. Chirac was elected in 1995 for seven years. He has called an early parliamentary election partly to renew the mandate for tight economic policies designed to take France into a single currency, the euro, from 1999.
Without referring directly to monetary union, Balladur said foreign policy was nowadays dominated by European actions -- and these in turn held sway over domestic economic policy.

"When we meet as 15 (European Union) countries and we say deficits should exceed or not exceed such a level, we are influencing the domestic economic policy of France and others. That is why I hope everything will be done to avoid a new cohabitation," Balladur said.

France has imposed economic rigour to reduce its deficit to three percent of national output and help qualify for the euro. Opposition Socialists, who took an unexpected lead in last Sunday's first round, say they oppose a new bout of austerity simply to fulfil a strict interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty on closer European union.
Asked whether he was ready to be prime minister again if the centre-right pulled back to win the election, Balladur did not rule himself out but refused to discuss his chances.
"That is a question which does not arise -- I don't say it is nonsense to ask it -- and if it does arise I will give it the appropriate answer at that time," he said.

Balladur is seen as an outsider for the job if Chirac's allies win the election. But socially-minded National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin has emerged in most newspapers as the front-runner, after setting up a last-minute "dream-team" ticket with free-marketing ex-finance minister Alain Madelin.
